subject: Vocabulary
topic: Phrasal Verbs — Meanings and Correct Usage (W10)

questions.stem: What does the phrasal verb 'call off' mean?

options.option_text: To call someone from a distance
To cancel or abandon a planned event
To shout loudly at someone
To make a phone call and disconnect

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Call off' = cancel or abandon (a planned event, strike, search). Example: 'The match was called off due to heavy rain.' Trap: 'call from a distance' confuses 'call off' with the literal sense of 'call'; 'disconnect' confuses 'call off' with ending a phone call. SSC tests this in sentence-completion questions.

questions.stem: What does 'break out' mean in the sentence: 'A fire broke out in the factory last night.'?

options.option_text: To escape from a confined place
To start suddenly and often violently
To destroy completely
To interrupt a conversation

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Break out' = (of something unpleasant like fire, war, disease) to begin suddenly. Example: 'Cholera broke out in the refugee camp.' The same phrase can mean 'escape' in different contexts (break out of prison), but with fire/war/disease, it means 'start suddenly.' Trap: 'escape' is the other meaning of 'break out' — context determines which applies.

questions.stem: What does 'bring up' mean in: 'She was brought up by her grandparents after her parents passed away.'?

options.option_text: To carry something upstairs
To raise and nurture a child
To introduce a topic in a discussion
To feel nauseous

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Bring up' (in the context of children) = raise, nurture, educate during childhood. Trap: 'introduce a topic' is another valid meaning of 'bring up' ('he brought up the issue of salary'), but in the given sentence, 'was brought up by grandparents' clearly refers to child-rearing; 'feel nauseous' is sometimes informally called 'bring up' (vomit) — but the context eliminates this.

options.option_text: To lean backwards accidentally
To return to a previous position
To rely on something as a last resort or backup
To decrease in value or quantity

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Fall back on' = use as a backup or last resort when primary options fail. Example: 'When the company collapsed, she fell back on her savings.' Trap: 'Return to a previous position' captures a literal element but not the idiomatic sense of emergency/backup dependency; 'decrease' confuses with 'fall back' (decline) which lacks 'on'.

options.option_text: To donate generously
To enter a room or building
To submit or hand over a document
To yield, surrender, or stop resisting

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Give in' = to yield to pressure, surrender, or accept defeat. Example: 'After hours of negotiation, the management gave in to the workers' demands.' Trap: 'hand over a document' is 'give in' in a literal sense (give in your homework), but the standard idiomatic meaning is yield/surrender — SSC typically tests the idiomatic sense.

options.option_text: To prevent something from falling
To maintain the same pace or standard as someone else
To repair or maintain a property
To save money regularly

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Keep up with' = maintain the same speed, level, or standard as someone or something else. Example: 'It is hard to keep up with the rapid changes in technology.' Trap: 'maintain a property' is 'keep up' (without 'with'); 'repair' misinterprets the phrase; 'save money' is an unrelated meaning.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'put off'.

options.option_text: She put off the candle before going to bed.
He put off the shoes before entering the temple.
They put off the meeting to next Friday.
The manager put off the new recruit as inefficient.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Put off' = postpone or delay. Example: 'Don't put off till tomorrow what you can do today.' Trap: A uses 'put out' (extinguish a flame); B uses 'take off' (remove footwear); D uses 'write off' or 'dismiss' — none of which is 'put off'. This tests whether students can distinguish between similar-sounding phrasal verbs.

options.option_text: To examine something from a height
To feel or show contempt or disdain for someone
To lower one's gaze in respect
To study something carefully

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Look down upon' = regard with a feeling of superiority or contempt; to treat as inferior. Example: 'It is wrong to look down upon people based on their economic status.' Trap: 'examine from a height' takes 'look down upon' literally; 'lower gaze in respect' is the physical opposite of its figurative meaning; 'study carefully' is 'look into'.

questions.stem: What does 'set out' mean in: 'The expedition set out for the summit at dawn.'?

options.option_text: To arrange objects neatly
To begin a journey or undertaking
To publish or display information
To establish a new rule

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Set out' (in the context of travel/journey) = begin a journey or undertaking. Example: 'They set out early to avoid traffic.' Trap: 'arrange objects' = 'set out' in another context (set out the chairs); 'publish information' = 'set out' in documents (the report sets out the findings) — but the given sentence's context of the expedition heading toward a summit clearly indicates 'begin a journey.'

questions.stem: Choose the correct meaning of 'run into' in: 'I ran into an old friend at the supermarket.'

options.option_text: To crash into someone with force
To encounter unexpectedly
To accumulate debts
To enter a building quickly

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Run into someone' = meet someone by chance/unexpectedly. Example: 'She ran into her former classmate at the airport.' Trap: 'crash into' is a literal meaning of 'run into'; 'accumulate debts' is another meaning of 'run into' (run into debt); 'enter quickly' uses 'run' literally. Context — a supermarket meeting — confirms the accidental encounter meaning.
